items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: had a hell of a band up there, Joe Wilder and Frank Galbraith and I'm just calling Jonesie

ctx.x: I was in the union and I see Lucky Millinder in the union, Local 802, it was on Sixth Avenue then, so he said, "What's going on over there?" So I says, "Well, the band's breaking up." He says, "That's what I heard." He says, "What are you going to do?" I said, "I can't do anything." I says, "I got three months before I can work." You know that law, like if a musician comes in, you know, he's got to put his -- if he's like from -- if he's not a 802 musician. You can put your transfer in, you can gig every night,…

So Lucky says, -- Lucky was tight with the union, you know. He's a big man down there. They tell me like during Christmastime, he looked like Santa Claus. He'd go into so many presents, everybody in the union got a big present from him. He didn't care anything about money. I want to tell you some things about Lucky, too, that I think you might like. He was a great man. And he says, "Well, do you want to come to work with me?" He said, "I'm working up to 845," had a hell of a band up there, Joe Wilder and Frank…

played -- had a hell of a brass section, good reed section. I said, "Man, I can't go to work. I'm just putting my transfer in today." I says, "I can't work on a --" He says, "Are you interested?" I says, "Yeah, but you know what happens if they catch me, you know?" They'll tear up your card and maybe won't let you come in the union. He said, "Don't worry about it." Well, I'd heard he was big with the union people. And so I went to work that night, Gary. And I worked six weeks at the 845. Now, I don't have but…
